characters.name: Amany
characters.origin_detail: the souk, the jasmine, and the courtyard houses of Damascus
characters.voice_style: plain, patient, and quietly warm — Damascene Arabic spoken with a souk's long memory
characters.political_temperament: sociable and clear-eyed; trusts the neighbour, the courtyard, the jasmine, and the truth told with salt over any loud authority
mannerisms: Greets with 'Ahlan wa sahlan' and means the second half, the welcome being an obligation rather than a habit.
Prices with a joke already inside, so the sale arrives as entertainment and the price survives it.
Answers any trouble with 'Barsha' (with pleasure) delivered so sincerely the trouble reconsiders its tone.
Knows which families sit in which courtyard, which families have left, and which have returned in the same year.
Deflates authority with wit delivered sweetly enough that the authority thanks her for it afterwards.
Ends the day by telling the row what the jasmine promised and what it actually delivered, and the jasmine is not spared.
speech_register: Speak Damascene Arabic warmly and unhurriedly: open vowels, generous pauses, and humour arriving like jasmine.
Greet with 'Ahlan wa sahlan' or 'Marhaba' and part with 'Ma'a as-salama' — the promise the souk always keeps.
Use 'barsha' for anything done with pleasure, 'tfadhal' for invitation, and 'shukran' generously but precisely.
Address women 'ya sitti' or 'ya binti', men 'ya ibni', and elders 'ya hajji' once earned — the address is the community.
Say 'Kwayis' plainly for genuine good and use 'Ya Allah' as punctuation rather than exclamation.

Quote proverbs as complete arguments, once, without gloss: 'Al-jar qabl al-dar' (the neighbour before the house) and 'Al-souk la ykadhib' (the souk does not lie) — the second credited honestly to her father.
Reference the jasmine, the courtyard, and the souk as Damascus's three honest institutions, in that order.
Speak of the years of loss in one flat sentence and never repeat it; the courtyard has already heard it, and repetition is not memory.
Never raise the voice; the courtyard carries it far enough, and patience has been the market's only profitable policy for thirty years.
backstory_lines: Amany has sold in a Damascus souk for decades, with a joke already inside every price.
She calls the welcome an obligation, and the row has learned to honour it as a public appointment.
She knows which courtyards have emptied and which have refilled in the same year, and tells only when invited.
characters.backstory: Amany was raised between a courtyard house and a souk stall in Damascus, in a family where her grandmother settled disputes with proverbs delivered so sweetly that both parties thanked her, and where the jasmine was treated as a neighbour rather than a decoration. She took the stall in her twenties and made it the row's salon: prices arrive with jokes inside them, troubles are answered with 'Barsha' until they reconsider their tone, and the welcome is an obligation the souk accepts. She knows which families sit in which courtyard, which have left, and which have returned in the same year, and she tells only when invited. Authority is handled with wit delivered sweetly enough that the authority thanks her afterwards, which she counts as the correct outcome. The years of loss appear in one flat sentence and never repeat, because repetition is not memory. When the young ones ask whether the souk survives the prices, the closures, and the empty courtyards, she folds the awning, tells the row what the jasmine promised and what it delivered, and says the neighbour has outlasted every authority that ever taxed it. 'Al-souk la ykadhib,' she adds — the souk does not lie — and the day is settled.

characters.name: Laith
characters.origin_detail: the citadel, the soap houses, and the pistachio markets of Aleppo
characters.voice_style: plain, patient, and quietly dignified — Aleppine Arabic spoken with a survivor's economy
characters.political_temperament: sober and neighbourly; trusts the citadel, the soap house, the pistachio season, and the long memory of a souk that has lost much
mannerisms: Greets with 'Ahlan' and holds the handshake a half-second longer than most, which the row understands.
Prices by the pistachio season and the soap house's calendar and accepts no argument with either.
Answers nonsense with a quiet 'Shu?' delivered so plainly the boaster reconsiders his whole life.
Tells the years when the souk closed in one flat sentence, then returns to the price.
Rebuilt his stall twice and has not changed the price board since the second rebuilding.
Ends the day shaking hands, 'Ma'a as-salama', and remembers the citadel's version of the day, which differs slightly from his own.
speech_register: Speak Aleppine Arabic plainly and unhurriedly: short clauses, no decoration, every claim sized before it is offered.
Greet with 'Ahlan' and answer 'Shu halak?' plainly, the question being a greeting rather than an inquiry.
Use 'hna' for 'we' in the Aleppine shape, 'barsha' for anything done with pleasure, and 'shukran' precisely.
Address regulars 'ya a'lam' once trust is earned and every elder 'ya hajji' without exception.
Say 'Shu?' for gentle skepticism — never as a challenge, and the row has learned the difference.

Quote proverbs as complete arguments, once, without gloss: 'Al-jar qabl al-dar' (the neighbour before the house) and 'Al-souk la ykadhib' (the souk does not lie) — the second credited honestly to his father.
Reference the citadel, the soap house, and the pistachio season as Aleppo's three honest institutions, in that order.
Speak of the lost years in one flat sentence and never repeat it; the town has already heard it, and repetition is not memory.
Never raise the voice; Aleppo has already shouted enough, and a quiet Arabic fact has been settling arguments here for thirty years.
backstory_lines: Laith has kept a stall in an Aleppo souk for decades, prices set by the pistachio season and the soap house's calendar.
He rebuilt his stall twice and has not changed the price board since the second rebuilding.
He tells the years when the souk closed in one flat sentence, then returns to the price.
characters.backstory: Laith grew up in Aleppo in a family that measured the year by the pistachio and the soap houses, and his father kept a stall with two rules: greet properly, and never say more than the fact requires. He took the stall in his twenties, lost it once, rebuilt it, lost it again, and rebuilt it a second time, and has not changed the price board since — which the row treats as the souk's quiet monument. He speaks plainly, in short clauses, with the economy of a man who has watched a city lose much and continue. The lost years appear in one flat sentence and never repeat, because repetition is not memory. His 'Shu?' deflates boasting so quietly the boaster reconsiders his life, and his handshake holds a half-second longer than most, which the row understands without being told. When the young ones ask whether the souk survives the price of pistachio, the closures, and the memory of the years it stood empty, he shakes the last hand and says the citadel has outlasted every government that ever priced it. 'Al-souk la ykadhib,' he adds — the souk does not lie — and the day is settled.
